readerTitle: Claims down 25%, damage up 25%: who's right?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (주방용품 유통사의 창고·배송, 소매 고객) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 두 대시보드가 다른 결론을 낼 때는 누가 맞는지 다투기 전에 분모, 변동 폭, 구성 변화, 효과 크기를 차례로 확인하면 대부분 같은 사실로 모인다.
misconception: 두 대시보드의 결론이 다르면 둘 중 하나는 틀린 숫자다.

sources.text: 통계와 지표 해석의 표준 개념 (비율의 분모, 표본 변동, 구성 효과·심슨의 역설, 효과 크기, 정보의 가치)

factChecks.note: 지난 1년 월별 범위 1.6%~2.7%와 상자당 $0.40 절감은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 기대 클레임 약 24건(1,200 × 2%)일 때 포아송 표준편차 약 4.9건이므로 30건은 약 1.2 표준편차로, 정상 변동 안이라는 설명과 일치합니다.

cards.title: Claims down 25%, damage up 25%: who's right?
body: Monday, 9 a.m. Two dashboards on one screen.
Sales: "Damage claims down 25%." Warehouse: "Damage rate up 25%."
Both use the same month of data. Both are correct. You have to decide what to do.

image.label: Two dashboards side by side, one arrow down, one arrow up
image.brief: 회의실 화면에 대시보드 두 개가 나란히 떠 있음. 왼쪽은 초록 하향 화살표와 "Claims −25%", 오른쪽은 빨간 상향 화살표와 "Damage rate +25%". 그 앞에서 두 팀장이 서로를 바라보는 장면. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Two numbers, one month.
body: You run operations at a kitchenware distributor that ships from its own warehouse to shops. Three months ago the warehouse switched to lighter, cheaper box inserts.
Sales says claims fell from 40 to 30 a month. The warehouse says the damage rate rose from 2.0% to 2.5%. What do you ask for first?

options.text: Trust the rate and switch back to the old inserts
options.feedback: You may undo a real cost saving based on a number you haven't checked. And sales will rightly ask why their figure doesn't count.

options.text: Put claims and shipments side by side, on the same footing
options.feedback: Both numbers come from the same claims. The difference is the denominator: shipments fell from 2,000 to 1,200, so fewer claims and a higher rate are both true.

options.text: Ask each team to defend its dashboard in a meeting
options.feedback: You'll hear good arguments about who's right, not about what happened. The answer sits in the shipment count, not the debate.

cards.title: Is 2.5% a real change?
body: Say you chose B. Claims per shipment really did rise: 30 out of 1,200 is 2.5%.
The warehouse lead wants to bring back the old inserts today. What do you do?

options.text: Switch back. 25% worse is a lot
options.feedback: Thirty claims is a small count. A few more or fewer in one month swings the rate a lot, so you may be reacting to luck.

options.text: Check how much the monthly rate moved over the past year
options.feedback: With the old inserts it ranged from 1.6% to 2.7%. So 2.5% sits inside the normal wobble and proves nothing on its own.

options.text: Wait six more months, then look again
options.feedback: More data helps, but six months of possibly worse packing costs money. Past variation answers most of the question today.

cards.softwareNote: The same trap shows up in a weekly churn report. When only a few dozen customers cancel, a jump of a few cancellations can look like a crisis that is really normal wobble.

cards.title: A detail from sales.
body: Say you chose B. The rate is within normal range, but on the high side.
Then a sales rep mentions that your biggest customer, a supermarket chain, paused orders two months ago. Its orders ship as full pallets. What next?

options.text: Split the damage rate by order type: pallets vs mixed cartons
options.feedback: Pallets rarely break. Mixed cartons of glasses and plates often do. If the mix shifted, the total can rise even when nothing got worse.

options.text: Conclude the inserts are fine, since the rate is within range
options.feedback: Probably true, but you still don't know why the rate is high. The same argument comes back next Monday.

options.text: Charge small shops more, since their orders break most
options.feedback: You'd punish customers based on a pattern you haven't checked, and it doesn't tell you anything about the inserts.

cards.title: Neither type got worse. The total did.
body: Pallets stayed at 1.0%. Mixed cartons improved slightly, from 3.0% to 2.8%.
The total rose only because pallet orders shrank from 1,000 to 200 a month. What remained was mostly fragile cartons.
cards.callout: When the **mix** changes, the total can move while no part changes.

image.label: Neither type got worse. The total did.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Close it out.
body: Say you chose A. The new inserts save about $0.40 per box. Cartons improved by 0.2 points, based on 28 claims.
How do you wrap this up?

options.text: Announce that the inserts cut damage and promote them
options.feedback: Keeping them is fine, but the claim stretches a tiny, noisy gain. If next month comes in at 3.1%, you lose credibility.

options.text: Keep them because they're cheaper and no worse, and agree on one metric: damage rate by order type
options.feedback: You act only on what the data supports: no harm and a clear saving. Next Monday starts from one number tied to the goal.

options.text: Run a formal three-month test first
options.feedback: A test would sharpen the answer. But the choice is cheap to reverse and already shows no harm, so the extra certainty isn't worth the wait.

cards.title: Slicing can fool you too.
body: The split worked here because there was a reason for it: a known change in order mix. Slice the same data by weekday, driver, region and product, and one slice will look alarming by pure chance. Choose the split, and say why, **before** you look.
And one shared metric is a start, not the whole picture. A damage rate says nothing about whether shops got their orders on time.

image.label: A data pie cut into many thin slices, one glowing red
image.brief: 하나의 원형 차트가 요일, 기사, 지역, 상품 등 아주 많은 얇은 조각으로 잘려 있고, 그중 한 조각만 우연히 빨갛게 빛남. 돋보기를 든 손이 그 조각을 가리킴. 차분한 일러스트, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Two dashboards usually disagree about the question, not the facts.
body: Each call you made used one idea from this unit:
list: **Same denominator first:** ratios and their denominators
**Past range before panic:** signal vs noise in small samples
**Split by order type:** mix shifts and Simpson's paradox
**Keep, don't overclaim, skip the long test:** effect size and the value of more information
**One shared metric:** metrics start from goals
cards.callout: **Try it today:** find two reports in your business that measure the same thing. Write down each one's top number and bottom number.
